questions.q: Let $e_1$ and $e_2$ be the eccentricities of the ellipse $\frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{\mathrm{~b}^2}+\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{25}=1 \quad$ and the hyperbola $\quad \frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{16}-\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{\mathrm{~b}^2}=1$, respectively. If $\mathrm{b} \lt 5$ and $\mathrm{e}_1 \mathrm{e}_2=1$, then the eccentricity of the ellipse having its axes along the coordinate axes and passing through all four foci (two of the ellipse and two of the hyperbola) is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{e}_1^2=1-\frac{\mathrm{b}^2}{25} \quad \mathrm{e}_2^2=1-\frac{\mathrm{b}^2}{16} \\ & \therefore \mathrm{e}_1^2 \mathrm{e}_2^2=1 \\ & \left(1-\frac{\mathrm{b}^2}{25}\right)\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{b}^2}{16}\right)=1 \\ & \Rightarrow 2+\frac{\mathrm{b}^2}{16}-\frac{\mathrm{b}^2}{25}-\frac{\mathrm{b}^2}{400}=1 \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{9 \mathrm{~b}^2}{400}=\frac{\mathrm{b}^4}{400} \\ & \mathrm{~b}^2=9 \\ & \frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{9}+\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{25}=1 \quad \frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{16}-\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{9}=0 \\ & \mathrm{e}_1 \sqrt{1-\frac{9}{25}} \\ & \mathrm{e}_1=\frac{4}{5}
\end{aligned}$
Focii : - $(0, \pm 4) \quad( \pm 5,0)$
ellipse passing through all four foci
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{x^2}{25}+\frac{y^2}{16}=1 \\ & e=\sqrt{1-\frac{16}{25}}=\frac{3}{5}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Let the hyperbola $H: \dfrac{x2}{a2} - \dfrac{y2}{b^{2}} = 1$~pass through the point  \left(2\sqrt{2}, - 2\sqrt{2}\right)$. A parabola is drawn whose focus is same as the focus of $H$ with positive abscissa and the directrix of the parabola passes through the other focus of $H$. If the length of the latus rectum of the parabola is e times the length of the latus rectum of $H$, where $e$ is the eccentricity of $H$, then which of the following points lies on the parabola?$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

$H: \dfrac{x2}{a2} - \dfrac{y2}{b^{2}} = 1$

So coordinates of foci will be : $S \left(ae, 0\right), S^{'} \left(-$ae, 0\right)$

Now foot of directrix of parabola will be~ \left(-ae, 0\right)$

Also focus of parabola is which is same as focus of~$H$~will be~ \left(ae, 0\right)$

Now, semi latus rectum of parabola $= \left|$SS^{'}\right| = 2ae$

Given, $4ae = $e \left(\dfrac{2b^{2}}{a})

$⇒ b^{2} = 2a^{2} . . . \left(1\right)$

Also given, \$lleft(2\sqrt{2}, ---2\sqrt{2})lies on $H: $\dfrac{x2}{a2} - \dfrac{y2}{b^{2}} =$1$

$⇒ $\dfrac{\left(2\sqrt{2}\right)2}{a2} - \dfrac{\left(2\sqrt{2}\right)2}{b^{2}} =$1$

$⇒ $\dfrac{1}{a2} - \dfrac{1}{b^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{8} . . . \left(2\right)$

Now from equation~ \left($1\right) \text{ and } \left(2\right)$~we get,

$a^{2} = 4, b^{2} = 8$

$∵ b^{2} = a^{2} \left($e^{2} - 1\right)$

$∴ e = $\sqrt{3}

So, the equation of parabola is $y^{2} = 4 $\times \left($ae\right)x⇒ y^{2} = 8\sqrt{3}x$

So, only~\$lleft(3\sqrt{3}, -$--6\sqrt{2})$~will satisfy the parabola~$y^{2} = 8\sqrt{3}x$

questions.q: The locus of the centroid of the triangle formed by any point $P$ on the hyperbola $16x^{2} - 9y^{2} + 32x + 36y - 164 = 0$& and its foci is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given hyperbola is

$16x^{2} - 9y^{2} + 32x + 36y - 164 = 0$

$⇒ 16\left(x + 1\right)2 - 9\left(y - 2\right)2 = 164 + 16 - 36$

$⇒ 16 \left(x + 1\right)2 - 9 \left($y - 2\right)2 = 144 . . . . \left($1\right)$

$⇒ $\dfrac{( x + 1{)}^{2}}{9} - \dfrac{( y - 2{)}^{2}}{16} =$1$

Compare the above~equation with~$⇒ $\dfrac{( x - h{)}^{2}}{a2} - \dfrac{( y - k{)}^{2}}{b2} =$1$

We get,~$h = - 1, k = 2, a^{2} = 9$~and~$b^{2} = 16$

$∴$~Eccentricity, $e = $\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{16}{9}} = \dfrac{5}{3}

We know that, focii are~ \left(h + ae, k\right)$~and~ \left(h - ae, k\right)$

Hence, focii are~$( 4, 2 )$~and~$( - 6, 2 )$

Let the centroid be $( h, k )$ &~$A ( \alpha, \beta )$be point on hyperbola

So $h = $\dfrac{\alpha - 6 + 4}{3},$k = $\dfrac{\beta + 2 + 2}{3}

$⇒ \alpha =3h + 2, \beta =3k - 4$

Put the values of~$\alpha, \beta$~in the equation \left($1\right)$,

16\left(\left($3h + 2\right) + 1\right)2 - $9\left(\left($3k - 4\right) - 2\right)2 = 144$

$⇒ 144 ( h + 1{)}^{2} - 81 ( k - 2{)}^{2} = 144$

$⇒ $16\left($h^{2} + 2h + 1\right) - $9\left($k^{2} - 4k + 4\right) = 16$

$⇒ 16h^{2} - 9k^{2} + 32h + 36k - 36 = 0$

So, the locus of the centroid is~

$16x^{2} - 9y^{2} + 32x + 36y - 36 = 0$

questions.q: Let ${e}_{1}$ be the eccentricity of the hyperbola $\dfrac{x2}{16} - \dfrac{y2}{9} = 1$ and ${e}_{2}$ be the eccentricity of the ellipse $\dfrac{x2}{a2} + \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1, a > b$, which passes through the foci of the hyperbola. If ${e}_{1}{e}_{2} = 1$, then the length of the chord of the ellipse parallel to the $x$-axis and passing through $( 0, 2 )$ is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The given equation of hyperbola is, $H: \dfrac{x2}{16} - \dfrac{y2}{9} = 1$

$⇒ {e}_{1} = \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{32}{42}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{16 + 9}{16}}$

$⇒ {e}_{1} = \dfrac{5}{4}$

Foci of this hyperbola is given by, $F \left(\pmae,0\right)$.

$⇒ F \left(\pm5, 0\right)$

It is given that, ${e}_{1}{e}_{2} = 1$

$⇒ {e}_{2} = \dfrac{4}{5}$

Also, ellipse is passing through $( \pm5, 0 )$

$⇒ \dfrac{52}{a2} + \dfrac{0}{b2} =1$

$⇒ \dfrac{25}{a2} =1$

$⇒ a^{2} = 25$

$⇒ a = 5$

Now, ${e}_{2} = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{b2}{a2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{4}{5} = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{b2}{25}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{16}{25} =1 - \dfrac{b2}{25}$

$⇒ \dfrac{b2}{25} = \dfrac{9}{25}$

$⇒ b^{2} = 9$

$∴ a = 5$ and $b = 3$

$E: \dfrac{x2}{25} + \dfrac{y2}{9} =1$

Putting, $y = 2$

$⇒ \dfrac{x2}{25} + \dfrac{4}{9} =1$

$⇒ \dfrac{x2}{25} = \dfrac{5}{9}$

$⇒ x^{2} = \dfrac{125}{9}$

$⇒ x = \pm \dfrac{5\sqrt{5}}{3}$

So, end points of chord are \left(\pm \dfrac{5\sqrt{5}}{3},2\right)$

Thus, length of chord $PQ$- is given by,

${L}_{PQ} = 2 \times \dfrac{5\sqrt{5}}{3}$

$⇒ {L}_{PQ} = \dfrac{10\sqrt{5}}{3}$

$

questions.q: Let $a > 0, b > 0$. Let $e$~and $l$~respectively be the eccentricity and length of the latus rectum of the hyperbola $\dfrac{x2}{a2} - \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1$. Let~$e^{'}$~and~$l^{'}$~respectively the eccentricity and length of the latus rectum of its conjugate hyperbola. If $e^{2} = \dfrac{11}{14}l$~and~\left(e^{'}\right)2 = \dfrac{11}{8}l^{'}$, then the value of $77a + 44b$ \text{ and } is equal to$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
By using eccentricty formula we get,

$e = \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{b2}{a2}}, l = \dfrac{2b^{2}}{a}$

Given~$e^{2} = \dfrac{11}{14}l$

So,~$1 + \dfrac{b2}{a2} = \dfrac{11}{14} \cdot \dfrac{2b^{2}}{a}$

$\dfrac{a^{2} + b^{2}}{a2} = \dfrac{11}{7} \cdot \dfrac{b2}{a} ⋯ \left(1\right)$

Also~$e^{'} = $\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{a2}{b2}},$l^{'} = $\dfrac{2a^{2}}{b}

Given~\left(e^{'}\right)2 = $\dfrac{11}{8}$l^{'}$

$1 + $\dfrac{a2}{b2} = \dfrac{11}{8} \cdot \dfrac{2a^{2}}{b}

\dfrac{a^{2} + b^{2}}{b2} = \dfrac{11}{4} \cdot \dfrac{a2}{b}$⋯ \left(2\right)$

Now equation~ \left(1\right) \div$equation~\left(2\right)$~we get,

$\dfrac{b2}{a2} = \dfrac{4}{7} \cdot \dfrac{b3}{a3}$

$∴ 7a = 4b ⋯ \left($3\right)$

From~ \left($2\right)$

\dfrac{\dfrac{16b^{2}}{49} + b^{2}}{b2} = \dfrac{11}{4} \cdot \dfrac{16b^{2}}{49b}

$∴ b = $\dfrac{4 \times 65}{11 \times 16}$⋯ \left(4\right)$

We have to find value of

$77a + 44b$

So,~$11\left(7a + 4b\right) = 11\left(4b + 4b\right) = 11 \times8b$

$∴$~Value of~$11 \times8b = 11 \times8 \times \dfrac{4 \times 65}{16 \times 11} =130$

questions.q: Let& ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ be the eccentricities of the ellipse~$\dfrac{x2}{25} + \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1  \left(b < 5\right)$ and the hyperbola~\dfrac{x2}{16} - \dfrac{y2}{b2} =$1$~respectively satisfying ${e}_{1}{e}_{2} = 1$. If $\alpha$~and~$\beta$~are the distances between the foci of the ellipse and the foci of the hyperbola respectively, then the ordered pair  \left(\alpha, \beta\right)$is equal to:$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
${e}_{1} = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{b2}{25}}$~and~${e}_{2} = \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{b2}{16}}$

Given~${e}_{1}{e}_{2} = 1$

$⇒ \left({e}_{1}{e}_{2}\right)2 = 1 ⇒ \left(1 - \dfrac{b2}{25}\right)\left(1 + \dfrac{b2}{16}\right) = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{b2}{16} - \dfrac{b2}{25} - \dfrac{b4}{25 \times 16} = 0$

$⇒ \dfrac{9}{16 \times 25}b^{2} - \dfrac{b4}{25 \times 16} = 0 ⇒ b^{2} = 9$

Thus,~${e}_{1} = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{9}{25}} = \dfrac{4}{5}$~and~${e}_{2} = \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{9}{16}} = \dfrac{5}{4}$

Therefore,~$\alpha = 2 \left(5\right)\left({e}_{1}\right) =8$~and~$\beta ==2 \left($4\right)\left({e}_{2}\right) =10$

$∴ \left(\alpha, \beta\right) = \left(8, 10\right)$

$

questions.q: If $5x + 9 = 0$ is the directrix of the hyperbola $16x^{2} - 9y^{2} = 144,$& then its corresponding focus is:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The equation of a hyperbola in standard form is& $\dfrac{x2}{a2} - \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1$~and its foci are~ \left(\pm ae, 0\right)$~and directrices are~$x = \pm \dfrac{a}{e} .$

The given equation of hyperbola is~$16x^{2} - 9y^{2} = 144, ⇒ \dfrac{x2}{9} - \dfrac{y2}{16} = 1$

$⇒ a^{2} = 9, b^{2} = 16$

Given, directrix of the hyperbola is $5x + 9 = 0, ⇒ x = - \dfrac{9}{5} .$

Hence, on comparing the directrix with the standard equation, we get~$\dfrac{a}{e} = \dfrac{9}{5}$

$⇒ \dfrac{3}{e} = \dfrac{9}{5}$

$⇒ e = \dfrac{5}{3}$

And, hence the required focus is \left(- ae, 0\right) = ( - 5, 0 ) .

$

questions.q: A hyperbola passes through the foci of the ellipse $\dfrac{x2}{25} + \dfrac{y2}{16} = 1$& and its transverse and conjugate axes coincide with major and minor axes of the ellipse, respectively. If the product of their eccentricities is one, then the equation of the hyperbola is:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
For ellipse ${e}_{1} = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{b2}{a2}} = \dfrac{3}{5}$

for hyperbola ${e}_{2} = \dfrac{5}{3}$

Let hyperbola be

$\dfrac{x2}{a2} - \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1$

$∵$ it passes through~ \left(3, 0\right) ⇒ \dfrac{9}{a2} = 1$

$⇒ a^{2} = 9$

$⇒ b^{2} = a^{2}\left(e^{2} - 1\right)$

$= 9\left(\dfrac{25}{9} - 1\right) = 16$

$∴$ Hyperbola is

$\dfrac{x2}{9} - \dfrac{y2}{16} = 1$

option \left(1\right)$

questions.q: Let $P$ be a point on the hyperbola $H: \dfrac{x2}{9} - \dfrac{y2}{4} = 1$, in the first quadrant such that the area of triangle formed by $P$ and the two foci of $H$ is $2\sqrt{13}$. Then, the square of the distance of $P$ from the origin is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Plotting the diagram of given data we get,

Given equation of hyperbola is $\dfrac{x2}{9} - \dfrac{y2}{4} = 1$.

$⇒ a^{2} = 9, b^{2} = 4$

We know that, $b^{2} = a^{2} \left(e^{2} - 1\right)$

$⇒ e^{2} = 1 + $\dfrac{b2}{a2}

$⇒ e^{2} = 1 + $\dfrac{4}{9}

$⇒ e^{2} = $\dfrac{13}{9}

$⇒ e = $\dfrac{13}{3}

Now, ${S}_{1}{S}_{2} = 2ae$

$⇒ {S}_{1}{S}_{2} = 2 \times3 \times $\sqrt{\dfrac{13}{3}}

$⇒ {S}_{1}{S}_{2} = $2\sqrt{13}

It is given that, area of $\Delta P{S}_{1}{S}_{2}$ is 2\sqrt{13}.

$⇒ $\dfrac{1}{2} \times \beta \times {S}_{1}{S}_{2} ===2\sqrt{13}

$⇒ $\dfrac{1}{2} \times \beta \tttimes2\sqrt{13} ===2\sqrt{13}

$⇒ $\beta =$2$

Since, \left(\alpha, \beta\right)lies on the hyperbola,

$⇒ $\dfrac{\alpha2}{9} - \dfrac{\beta2}{4} =$1$

$⇒ $\dfrac{\alpha2}{9} -$1 = 1$

$⇒ {α}^{2} = 18$

$⇒ $\alpha ==3\sqrt{2}$

Distance of $P$ from origin is given by,

$OP = \sqrt{{α}^{2} + {β}^{2}}$

$⇒ OP = \sqrt{18 + 4}$

$⇒ OP = \sqrt{22}$

$⇒ OP^{2} = 22$

$

questions.q: Let one focus of the hyperbola $\mathrm{H}: \frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{\mathrm{a}^2}-\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{\mathrm{~b}^2}=1$ be at $(\sqrt{10}, 0)$ and the corresponding directrix be $\mathrm{x}=\frac{9}{\sqrt{10}}$. If e and $l$ respectively are the eccentricity and the length of the latus rectum of H , then $9  \left(\mathrm{e}^2+$l\right)$ is equal to:$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{ae}=\sqrt{10} \text { and } \frac{\mathrm{a}}{\mathrm{e}}=\frac{9}{10} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}^2=9 \text { and } \mathrm{e}=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{3} \\ & \text { Now } \quad $\begin{aligned} & (\mathrm{ae})^2=\mathrm{a}^2+\mathrm{b}^2 \\ & 10=9+\mathrm{b}^2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{~b}^2=1 \\ & \\ & \ell=\frac{2 \mathrm{~b}^2}{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{2(1)}{3} \\ \Rightarrow & 9\left(\mathrm{e}^2+\ell\right) \\ & =9\left(\frac{10}{9}+\frac{2}{3}\right) \\ & =10+6 \\ & =16\end{aligned}$\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Let $\dfrac{x2}{a2} + \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1, a > b$ be an ellipse, whose eccentricity is $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and the length of the latus rectum is $\sqrt{14}$. Then the square of the eccentricity of $\dfrac{x2}{a2} - \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1$ is:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$Given: Length of latus rectum of ellipse is $\sqrt{14}$.

$⇒ \dfrac{2b^{2}}{a} = \sqrt{14} . . . \left(i\right)$

Also, eccentricity is given as \dfrac{1}{2}

$⇒ $\dfrac{1}{2} = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{b2}{a2}}

$⇒ $\dfrac{1}{2} =$1 - $\dfrac{b2}{a2}

$⇒ $\dfrac{1}{2} =$1 - $\dfrac{a\sqrt{14}}{2a^{2}}

$⇒ $\dfrac{- 1}{2} = - \dfrac{14}{2a}

$⇒ a = $\sqrt{14}

$⇒ a^{2} = 14, b^{2} = 7$

Now, ${e}_{H} = $\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{b2}{a2}}

$⇒ {e}_{H} = $\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{1}{2}}

$⇒ {e}_{H} = $\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}

$⇒ \left({e}_{H}\right)2 = \dfrac{3}{2}$

$

questions.q: Let $H$ be the hyperbola, whose foci are  \left(1 \pm \sqrt{2}, 0\right)$ and eccentricity is $\sqrt{2}$. Then the length of its latus rectum is:$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given the foci points of a hyperbola are& \left(1 \pm \sqrt{2}, 0\right)$

So,~$S \left(1 + $\sqrt{2},$0\right), S^{'} \left($1 - \sqrt{2},0\right)$

$SS^{'} = 2ae = ( 1 + \sqrt{2} ) - (1 - \sqrt{2} )$

$⇒ 2ae = 2\sqrt{2}$

$⇒ 2 \timesa $\times $\sqrt{2} ===2\sqrt{2}, \left(\text{given}e = \sqrt{2}\right)$

$⇒ a = 1$

Since~$b^{2} = a^{2} ( e^{2} - 1 )$

$⇒ b^{2} = 1 ( 2 - 1 ) = 1$

So,~the latus~rectum of a hyperbola is given by,

L.R. $= \dfrac{2b^{2}}{a}$

L.R.~$= 2

$

questions.q: For some $\theta \in \left(0, \dfrac{π}{2}\right),$ if the eccentricity of the hyperbola, $x^{2} - y^{2}\sec^{2}\theta = 10$ is $\sqrt{5}$ times the~eccentricity of the ellipse, $x^{2}\sec^{2}\theta + y^{2} = 5,$ then the length of the latus rectum of the ellipse, is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
For hyperbola& $\dfrac{x2}{10} - \dfrac{y2}{10\cos^{2}\theta} = 1$

The eccentricity of the hyperbola~${e}_{H} = \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{b2}{a2}} = \sqrt{1 + \cos^{2}\theta}$

For ellipse~$\dfrac{x2}{5\cos^{2}\theta} + \dfrac{y2}{5} = 1$

The eccentricity of an ellipse~${e}_{E} = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{b2}{a2}} = \sqrt{1 - \cos^{2}\theta} = sin\theta$

Given,~${e}_{H} = \sqrt{5}{e}_{E}$

$⇒ 1 + \cos^{2}\theta = 5\sin^{2}\theta ⇒ \cos^{2}\theta = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Now,~the length of the latus rectum~of an ellipse~$= \dfrac{2b^{2}}{a} = \dfrac{10\cos^{2}\theta}{5} = \dfrac{20}{3\sqrt{5}} = \dfrac{4\sqrt{5}}{3}$

questions.q: If a directrix of a hyperbola centered at the origin and passing through the point  \left(4, - 2\sqrt{3}\right)$ is $5x = 4\sqrt{5}$~and~its eccentricity is $e$, then:$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let equation of hyperbola is $\dfrac{x2}{a2} - \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1$

$∴$ It passes through \left(4, - 2\sqrt{3}\right) ⇒ \dfrac{16}{a2} - \dfrac{12}{b2} = 1$

$⇒ 16 - 12 \times \dfrac{a2}{b2} = a^{2} . . . \left(1\right)$

Equation of directrix is $x = $\dfrac{a}{e} = \dfrac{4}{5},given in question.

$⇒ a^{2} = $\dfrac{16}{5}$e^{2} . . . \left(2\right)$

And we know that $b^{2} = a^{2} \left(e^{2} - 1\right)$

$⇒ $\dfrac{b2}{a2} =$e^{2} - 1 . . . \left($3\right)$

$∴$ From~ \left($1\right), \left($2\right) \text{ and } \left(3\right)$

$16 - $\dfrac{12}{e^{2} - 1} = \dfrac{16}{5}$e^{2}$

$⇒ 16e^{2} - 16 - 12 = $\dfrac{16e^{2}}{5} \left(e^{2} - 1\right)$

$⇒ 4e^{4} - 24e^{2} + 35 = 0$

questions.q: Let the foci of the ellipse& $\dfrac{x2}{16} + \dfrac{y2}{7} = 1$~and the hyperbola~$\dfrac{x2}{144} - \dfrac{y2}{α} = \dfrac{1}{25}$& coincide. Then the length of the latus rectum of the hyperbola is:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given equation of ellipse& $\dfrac{x2}{16} + \dfrac{y2}{7} = 1$

Now finding eccentricity~$= \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{7}{16}} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

So, foci~$≡ \left(\pmae, 0\right) ≡ \left(\pm$3, 0\right)$

Now, hyperbola:~x^{2}\left(\dfrac{144}{25}) --$y^{2}\left(\dfrac{α}{25}\right) =1$

Eccentricity will be~$= \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{α}{144}} = \dfrac{1}{12}\sqrt{144 + \alpha}$

Foci~$≡ \left(\pmae, 0\right) ≡ \left(\pm \dfrac{12}{5} \cdot \dfrac{1}{12}\sqrt{144 + \alpha},0\right)$

Given foci coincide then~$3 = \dfrac{1}{5}\sqrt{144 + \alpha}⇒ \alpha =81$

Hence, hyperbola is~$\dfrac{x2}{\left(\dfrac{12}{5}\right)2} - \dfrac{y2}{\left(\dfrac{9}{5}\right)2} =1$

Length of latus rectum~$= 2\dfrac{b2}{a} =2 \cdot \dfrac{\dfrac{81}{25}}{\dfrac{12}{5}} = \dfrac{27}{10}$

$

questions.q: Let the foci and length of the latus rectum of an ellipse $\dfrac{x2}{a2} + \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1$, $a > b$ be  \left(\pm 5, 0\right)$ and $\sqrt{50}$, respectively. Then, the square of the eccentricity of the hyperbola $\dfrac{x2}{b2} - \dfrac{y2}{a^{2}b^{2}} = 1$ equals$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$Given,

Ellipse $\dfrac{x2}{a2} + \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1$

And its focii $≡ \left(\pm5, 0\right)$ and its latusrectum \dfrac{2b^{2}}{a} = \sqrt{50}

So, $ae = 5$ and $b^{2} = $\dfrac{5\sqrt{2}a}{2}

Now, using the formula eccentricity we get,

$b^{2} = a^{2}\left(1 - e^{2}\right) = $\dfrac{5\sqrt{2}a}{2}

$⇒ a\left(1 - e^{2}\right) = $\dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}\left$\${\text{as}$a \ne 0\right\}$

$⇒ \dfrac{5}{e}\left(1 - e^{2}\right) = \dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}$

$⇒ \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{2}e^{2} = e$

$⇒ \sqrt{2}e^{2} + e - \sqrt{2} =0$

$⇒ \sqrt{2}e^{2} + 2e - e - \sqrt{2} =0$

$⇒ $\ssqrt{2}e\left(e + $\sqrt{2}\right) --$1\left($1 + \sqrt{2}\right) =0$

$⇒ \left($e + \sqrt{2}\right)\left(\sqrt{2}e - 1\right) = 0$

$∴ e \ne - \sqrt{2}; e = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ a = 5\sqrt{2}$and $b = 5$

Now, finding eccentricity of hyperbola,

$\dfrac{x2}{b2} - \dfrac{y2}{a^{2}b^{2}} =1$

We know that formula of eccentricity of hyperbola is given by, $B^{2} = A^{2} \left({eH}^{2} -$1\right)$ where $A^{2} = b^{2} & B^{2} = a^{2}b^{2}$

$⇒ a^{2}b^{2} = b^{2} \left({e}_H^{2} - 1\right)$

$⇒ a^{2} = \left({e}_H^{2} - 1\right)$

$⇒ 50 = \left({e}_H^{2} -$1\right)$

$⇒ {e}_H^{2} = 51

$

comparing with $3 x^2-y^2-\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma=0$, we get $\mathrm{a}^2=1$ and $\alpha=36, \beta=4$ and $\gamma=101$
$\therefore \alpha+\beta+\gamma=141$
